name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
title: Charles Spurgeon: a pulpit and an open door for children
description: Spurgeon and the beginning of the Stockwell orphanage in 1867: preaching, pastoral training and practical compassion, with documentary sources.

sections.heading: A well-known voice in London
paragraphs: Charles Haddon Spurgeon came to the ministry at New Park Street while still very young. His preaching drew a growing congregation and, in 1861, the Metropolitan Tabernacle opened. The library that preserves his legacy also describes the ongoing publication of his sermons and his work in training pastors.

His life’s work included books, teaching and care for vulnerable people. The Pastors’ College and the Stockwell orphanage are part of that story. The portrait of Spurgeon is incomplete when it focuses only on his ability to speak before a crowd and leaves out the needs his community met.

sections.heading: Compassion needed a home
paragraphs: The Stockwell orphanage was established in 1867. The Spurgeon Library’s research on his social activity highlights Anne Hillyard’s support for the project. The work shows cooperation among the congregation, its leaders and those who gave resources to take in children who needed a home.

Preaching and material care were both present in the same ministry. The Spurgeon Library’s biographical source allows us to place the orphanage within a wider activity. There is no need to credit him with limitless goodness or to use spectacular figures in order to recognize the importance of the work he undertook.

reflection: 1 John 3:16–18 calls us to love in action and in truth. That teaching offers a framework for thinking about the relationship between the public word and concrete care. A congregation can listen to faithful sermons and ask itself, at the same time, how it responds to the needs of its neighbors and its most vulnerable members.

The Stockwell story invites us to an organized compassion. Children need constant protection, clear responsibilities and people prepared to care for them. Initial generosity must become safe and lasting work. Remembering Spurgeon can encourage both Bible teaching and care for those who need a place to live and grow.
review_note: Sermons and famous quotations are not copied. Figures of reach are omitted, and the 1867 founding is distinguished from later expansion.
